newsitem.title: USA: API warns against US govt role in heat oil market.
newsitem.headline: API warns against US govt role in heat oil market.

text.p: The U.S. government would drive heating oil prices higher instead of lower if it tried to buy heating oil now for sales to consumers later this winter, as suggested by a group of northeastern lawmakers, the American Petroleum Institute said Tuesday.
"If you had the government purchase that distillate for the purpose of building stocks, ... you would clearly raise the price of distillate," said API president Charles DiBona.
With futures prices for heating oil much lower than current market prices -- market backwardation -- refiners have little incentive to pay the costs of storing heating oil.

"If the (government's) intention were to dump the product in the market two or three months hence, you would expect the futures market to reflect that as even more steep backwardation than we currently have, which is very steep by historical standards," DiBona told reporters.
"It seems like a tremendously counterproductive thing to attempt," said the president of API, which represents major oil companies.
His comments closely matched those of petroleum marketers last week.

Northeast lawmakers two weeks ago raised concern about the low level of heating oil stocks available going into this winter and asked the Clinton administration to consider taking steps to keep a lid on prices.

Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary has not yet replied their letter, but is due to meet Tuesday afternoon with Democratic Sens. Joseph Lieberman and Christopher Dodd of Connecticut, and Rep. Joe Kennedy of Massachusetts, to discuss the potential for price spikes.
Energy Department officials have so far said they did not plan to enter the heating oil market.
Consumer group Citizen Action, which first raised the alarm over heating oil stocks, Tuesday accused the administration of selling out to refiners.

"We are extraordinarily disappointed with the Department of Energy's and the Clinton Administration's refusal to address this emergency heating oil supply situation that U.S. oil refiners have created," said the group's energy policy director, Ed Rothschild.
